utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 25th of June, 2008. Good morning, Witness. Good morning to the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives and to all the people. Mr. Usher, can you check? Witness, can you hear me now? Fine. I was greeting everybody. I do this again in order not to forget anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good morning again, Witness. Mr. Registrar, you have the floor because you have some IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Akmadzic, Mile. The list submitted by 1D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00809. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00810. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 00811. And the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 00812. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Karnavas, in order to save time, I understand that during proofing, there were new documents that were submitted and you intend to use them. When you do, you will ask for the documents to be added to the 65 ter list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In fact, I was planning on reading the list of documents now so we have it all and I will begin. It's 1D 02941, 1D 02942, 1D 02943, 1D 02944, 1D 02945, 1D 02946, 1D 02947, 1D 02948, and 1D 02949. And I should also note that after leaving here yesterday, we reduced the documents that we probably will be discussing with the witness so hopefully I will be able to finish my direct examination in two and a half hours or so. That's my game plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At any rate, I'm not going to intervene so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Primorac.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we left off with this one document, 1D 02689, and I'd ask you to look at it. It was -- it's an agreement on the manner of conducting payment transactions in the dinar balance between legal entities and national persons from the Republic of Croatia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia. I had asked you in particular to look at Article 2 and tell us whether you can give us your interpretation of this document, in particular provide us with any comments.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the document pertains to the time before I became Minister of Finance. It has to do with the first payments agreement between the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia and more specifically, it deals with part of the subject matter regulated in the payments agreement, namely, how the balances that already were there on the 31st of December, 1991, would be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just quick question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One quick question. Why would such an agreement be necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I tried to explain that at the moment when the former Yugoslavia was falling apart, there were many outstanding claims among the different republics. It wasn't only Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia but all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Since they did not have enough foreign currency to pay these outstanding debts, then through agreements such as this one, it was regulated how this would be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I notice that your chair is a bit low and I've also noticed that you're rather tall. Are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can raise the chair a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a good thing that you're taking care of me, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01339. This is a decree law on money of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We see at the bottom it's dated 2 July 1992, and from the very first article, it talks about monetary units and means of payment in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be the dinar issued by the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you explain to us about this particular decree based on your experience and knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the key documents for bringing about monetary independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a decree law on the establishment of the money of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Until then, until the 15th of August, what was in circulation was the money issued by the central bank, that is to say the National Bank of Yugoslavia. That was money that was in existence throughout the former Yugoslavia. Through this decree law and through the other documents that followed, Bosnia and Herzegovina basically wanted to make itself independent from the national bank, the central bank of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before we get to the other documents, do you know whether this decree was actually implemented and if so, at what time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree was implemented not fully, perhaps I can put it in those terms. In August 1992 in this file of documents, it will probably be there, so this is the legal basis for bringing the money in. How this will be implemented in actual fact what the money would look like, what -- how it would be distributed, all of that was regulated in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 02945, 2945. We see that it's dated at the bottom July 13, 1992. At the top it's Republic of Croatia Ministry of Finance as the buyer and then the government of the Republic of Bosnia as the seller and this is a contract or advance payment for purchase of various goods and we see the actual amount of -- I believe it's 500 million Croatian dinars. Do you know anything about this particular document, sir, and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'm not the person who signed it because at that time, I was in Sarajevo and as you know, Sarajevo was under blockade. This document was signed in Zagreb. On behalf of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was Mr. Krsticevic, the trade minister who signed it on the authority vested in him by the government. It had to do with an advance payment that the Republic of Croatia gave to Bosnia and Herzegovina primarily in order to buy humanitarian aid supplies that were arriving in the port of Ploce, different food supplies such as flour, sugar for the general population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the next document, and for Your Honours, I'm going to be covering four documents together with three other documents with this one and I'll read out the numbers so you can have them handy but we'll go one through one, or one by one. It's 1D 01773 and then I will be discussing 1769, then going on to 1765 and then 1764 but we'll start off with 1773. If you could look at this, sir. We see that the title of it is, Platform for regulating the relationship with the Republic of Croatia. Are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know when about this document was generated, on or about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was prepared during the first half of July 1992. It was used as a platform for discussions with the Republic of Croatia that were being prepared. I'm not sure of the date but I think that these talks were held around the 20th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to draw your attention to the last paragraph of paragraph one after the six listed items where it says and I'll read for everyone's convenience, "Alongside these issues that must be resolved as soon as possible, it is also necessary to discuss the relationship between two sovereign states in order to commence with the drafting of certain agreements." Now, keeping that in mind, sir, if we go to the next page under item number 2 where it talks about money transfers and financial cooperation and, again, the very last paragraph of that page, again I will read it, it says, "Within the framework of financial cooperation and establishment of a joint bank should be initiated that would encourage the development of cooperation between business entities." Can you please comment on this, sir, if you are in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That part of the platform regulates financial cooperation with the Republic of Croatia, that is part of the material prepared by my ministry. The idea was to speed up or normalise, if we can put it that way, the economic relations between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia. It says here that a joint bank was supposed to be established. In linguistic terms it can be interpreted in different ways, in the singular or in the plural, but here it seems to be in the singular. This would speed up and normalise relations between the two countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01769. This is a feasibility study on economic justifiability of the funding of the Hrvatska Banka Mostar, a joint stock company, and this is dated November 1992. And my first question is are you familiar with this bank, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't seen this document before. This is the first time I see it. But as Minister of Finance of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I did attend the founding assembly of this bank in Medjurgorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us a little bit about that event?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a standard founding assembly. There were companies both from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina that founded the bank with their own capital so this was an assembly that dealt with the establishment of the bank, its leadership, everything that one does when establishing a bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it back then as it is today, to some extent, banks are regulated by the government.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Regulations on the establishment of banks, that is to say, the entire procedure of establishing banks is dealt with by the central bank of the country concerned. In this case, the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the one that carried out the formal part of reviewing documents and issuing licences. As for the government and my presence there, this was political support in terms of cooperation with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I guess I slipped because in my terminology, government would also include that. But given your answer, let's look at the next document, 1D 01765, 1765, and here we see that this is a decision and it's permission is granted to establish the mixed ownership bank, Hrvatska Banka Mostar. And we see at the bottom Dr. Stiepo Andrijic who was the governor of the national bank of Bosnia which would be, then, consistent with what you just told us, that he would be the central bank or the national bank that would be regulating private banks or mixed banks; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is approval. Actually this is an authorisation provided to the bank to engage in certain operations, however, everything that is important in terms of regulating the work of the bank falls under the authority of the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in this case Governor Andrijic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the next document 1D 01764, 1764, we see that this is a decision by Dr. Stiepo Andrijic, who was the governor of the national bank, and it's the decision that the mixed ownership bank, or Hrvatska Banka, is hereby granted authorisation to conduct international money transfers and credit warranty activities. So I take it this sort of an implementing document; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm not in a position to answer. Could you please repeat your question because I didn't seem to hear the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that -- based on the earlier document we now see a document related to Hrvatska Banka and here we see from item one that this bank is granted authorisation to conduct international money transfers and credit-warranty activities. So this again would show that this bank is being regulated by the national bank.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The national bank regulates the work of all banks. This is a decision that is issued in order to allow the bank to engage in foreign economic relations. In most cases, for this kind of work, that is to say, payments with foreign countries, a special licence has to be issued because the national bank has to realise or, rather, establish that the commercial bank is properly equipped with the right personnel as well to carry out this kind of work. In this case, the central bank assured itself of the fact that this bank indeed was capable of handling such work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Karnavas, I did not want to put questions but given the relevance of the topic, I have to. I'm about to ask a question of this witness. Looking at this document, Witness, there is one conclusion that can be drawn. This Hrvatska Banka bank, apparently seated in Mostar since I can see Mostar next to this name, is granted authorisation by the National Bank Of Bosnia and Herzegovina to operate in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to have various activities including credit activities transfer activities, also a loan, lending activity. So based on this authorisation which seems to be sort of rather broad in its scope, does this mean that as of the date of this document, that is, 10th of November, 1992, in Mostar and around Mostar as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Croatian dinar going through this bank is going to be allowed to circulate freely and possibly be in an economic position of prime importance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is general approval for carrying out foreign economic relations so it pertains to all the countries with which it -- the bank has relations of correspondence as it is called, so it has to do with all the foreign currencies that the bank is authorised to deal with. That is my understanding of the matter and this is customary practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are speaking about foreign currencies but could the Croatian dinar also transit through the bank and based on this, could the bank lend money to a Mostar citizen or business or company not in a foreign currency but in Croatian dinars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know about these things, at that time, the Croatian dinar was a foreign currency for Bosnia and Herzegovina so the bank, depending on its rules, I don't know, but I assume that the bank could have allowed so-called foreign currency credits, that is to say, in Croatian dinars and in Deutschemark and any other foreign currency if it did indeed grant approval for credits in foreign currencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to follow-up from that question. At this point in history, what was the official currency circulating in Bosnia and Herzegovina and what was its value as a currency, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about November 1992. At the time, officially, the official foreign currency in -- or rather the official currency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the dinar issued by the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What its actual value was is subject to interpretation especially in terms of different areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina but basically it wasn't all that valuable. As for the value of other currencies that were in circulation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it depended on the situation and on the area involved, that is to say, how much money was in a particular area and also how many goods could be purchased in the area involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And how much value would it have outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the dinar of Bosnia and Herzegovina? It was a typical non-convertible currency. I don't know if anyone accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if we go to the next document, 1D 02047. This is a decree law on the application of the law on the financing of general social needs. If you could just look at that very briefly and I will be asking you to comment primarily on Article 2 and Article 4. So if you could just look at those two Articles very briefly and then maybe even Article 15. Are you familiar with this decree, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am familiar with this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at Article 2, under 1, we see that, The general social needs of the socio-political communities during an imminent threat of war and during the state of war shall be and it says, "The financing of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." My first question would be what is a socio-political community? What was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a term that was handed down to us by the previous system and no wonder, this was 1992. It surprised everything to catch in the simplest possible terms, it comprised all of the bodies of government in Bosnia and Herzegovina ranging from the municipalities to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself with all its institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 4, it says, "The needs referred to in Article 2 of this decree shall be financed by the socio-political community from the available resources determined in the war budget." Then it talks about a priority being given to armed forces. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean paragraph 1 or paragraph 2 of this Article? The first sentence or the second sentence or perhaps both?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. I have to provide a brief introduction. Each socio-political community, which is what it's called in Article 2, meaning a municipality or state and so on and so forth had or was supposed to have a war budget. The war budget included various sources of financing, income, the expenditure, that sort of thing. This Article tells us that each socio-political community can survive on its budget depending on how much money there is in that budget. There needs to be a balance. That's the first sentence. The second sentence tells us that based on such a modality of financing, priority should be given to the purposes of the armed forces, the consequences of war as well as the health and social security of the population which I believe is self-implicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 15, if you could help us with this article. Here it says, "The war budget of a socio-political community shall allocate resources for public enterprises on the basis of the opinion of the competent administrative organ."

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an Article that -- well, I'll try to remember what it was exactly that we were trying to say by this Article at the time. There was a lot of discussion going on, this was a time of war, there were many ideas floating about. This wasn't a system in which all the laws could be applied and so on and so forth. I think the Article was in reference to a situation of this kind. The republic or rather the war budget of the socio-political community needed to have certain funds to assist public companies. When I say public companies, I mean those pertaining to infrastructures such as the railroads, the forestry companies, the water supply companies and so on and so forth whenever there was damage to their equipment, to their communications of such a kind that the companies could no longer bank roll these projects from their own budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could slow down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's the best we can always do. Now, if we look at Article 20 and then we'll leave this document. First let's look at Article 20. It says "During an imminent threat of war and during a state of war, the socio-political community may determine new sources of revenue and abolish the existing ones; change i.e., increase, lower and abolish tax rates; determine tax relief and the exemption of certain taxpayers and determine the conditions and manner of use of resources intended for financing general social needs during an imminent threat of war and during a state of war." Could you please comment on this article? What was its intentions?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in my opinion a typical wartime article. Given the conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time there wasn't a lot of income that was regular and that a state of or some of the socio-political communities would have had available to them in peacetime. The economy was in tatters, the taxes weren't coming in regularly and in order to at least to some extent make it possible for the socio-political communities to balance their budgets, this provision gives them a possibility to amend the existing regulations when it came to their income. They now were entitled to get new sources of income through new avenues and modalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go to the next document, this is a rather different topic and again we're going to be covering several documents with this. We'll start off with 1D 02941. If you look at this document, we see at the bottom it's 6 August 1992, and it's titled, "Measures and activities to ensure means for survival of the population of RBH." If you could -- are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I worked on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you only -- we've only translated the very first page although we could certainly -- we will translate the rest but as this is the one of the documents we received from you, isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said that you worked on this document so you would be an ideal person to tell us exactly what this document is all about and what was its intentions.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is one of the documents of its kind. I'm not sure if we will be coming across more like these, we probably will. This was August 1992. Sarajevo was entirely under siege. Winter was encroaching and winter can be fierce in Bosnia. We tried to set up a staff, an HQ, I think that's what it's called, a government staff, if you like, that would try to make sure the population survived the winter. This is one of such documents and it envisaged measures and activities to be taken. This is a platform, if you like, envisaging measures to be taken. After that, there would be more specific programmes as to who should do what and when and such programmes as to who we would be talking to abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document and that is 1D 02697. This will tie in with your -- the last sentence of your answer. We see this is a note, it's dated 24 August 1992. It's from a meeting of the staff responsible for collecting funds for the needs of the population of RBH. We see under number 4 your name. And then if we go to the second page under AD 2, towards the middle of it, it says, "In order to involve the Catholic church in the available activities, it is necessary to conduct preliminary talks with the archbishop of -- I need some help Vrhbosna, Vinko Puljic. The prime minister Jure Pelivan and the finance minister Dr. Zarko Primorac will conduct these talks." Then it goes on, "In order to involve the Jewish organisations in this activity, the finance minister Dr. Zarko Primorac will conduct the talks with their president, Ceresnjes. Thank you. I'm having some problems. We can see others have been designated other tasks, so could you comment on this document a little bit, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, in order to implement this platform or programme to collect funds for the survival of the population, a special staff was set up which comprised for the most part leading ministers from different sectors of the economy, members of the government and a number of other people too. The staff would meet from time to time to consider measures that were taken and that remained to be taken. Specifically, I have two responsibilities here, one being to talk to the Catholic church and the other being to talk to the Jewish community in Sarajevo. I would, however, like to remind you of one thing because we will probably be becoming across another document later on at later stage that will show you that we had a lot of other commitments not just the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this staff, I had at least five or six other commitments and responsibilities that I was given, not just myself but all the other members of the staff too. This part that is in reference to these two talks, I remember that I talked to Mr. Ceresnjes. I also have to tell you that I don't remember talking to the archbishop, whether I talked to him or not is not something that I can say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the purpose was to get assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to try and mobilise all the available resources not just in Bosnia and Herzegovina but also and above all, resources outside Bosnia and Herzegovina because in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no such thing. The intention was to ask these two to go and talk to these two and then ask these two gentlemen and the rest after them to try to enlist the assistance of all of their foreign contacts and helpers to aid Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document 1D 02696. And I think this is sort of a follow-up to your previous answer which -- we see here is the programme and again we see your name and the other names of those individuals and their responsibilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the programme containing specific responsibilities and commitments until the 30th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go to 1D 02694. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a document that is part of the work of the survival staff. In order to have in the most general idea as to what our resources were at the time, understandably, we had to draw up a document to see what there was, what was available to us, what we could expect and what the basic needs were that we had to provide for over the next few months. This document shows you the financial resources that were available to us at the time or that could possibly have been available to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to -- probably in your binder skip forward a little bit. I'm going to go to 1D 02709. 1D 02709. If you look at the yellow stickies or posties or whatever you want to call them. If you wish, we can have the usher provide you with ...

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that might be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what it's about. I don't recognise the format but I know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the second page at the name, we see Jure Pelivan, he was the prime minister at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the very last paragraph, it talks about some sort of a delegation having a meeting on September 5th and 25th of 1992. So do you know what delegation Mr. Pelivan is talking about and can you help us a little bit because we don't have a date on this document. So I can only assume that it must have been before September 5 that this was generated and sent to the president of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a document that is part of the survival programme. One of the measures adopted at the time was for the prime minister to dispatch letters to several addressees in the world explaining the situation and requesting their assistance, to put it in the simplest of terms. This document is about the request that was made to the president of the European Commission to receive the Bosnian delegation, the BH delegation between the 5th and the 25 of September, the delegation was to be headed by a member of the Presidency, Dr. Ganic and I was a member of the delegation. We went to those talks, we discussed the population survival programme but it wasn't at this point in time. I think it was a lot later. I might even be able to remember the date, but it could have been possibly some time in late October.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the other date that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What might have been the other date, sir, because it wasn't picked up?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was between the end of October and the first decade of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we look at 1D 02712 and this would be the last document within this chapter. We see a survival programme for the population of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period 1 November 1992 to 30 June 1993. At the bottom of the page, we see Sarajevo, 1 November 1992. Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I didn't work on this document but it was a component of the activities taken by the survival staff. This is something that Mr. Ganic and I used for our presentation in terms of the needs of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the European commission. And I think I've given you a date already; I think it was sometime in the first half of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Again I'll ask you to slow down --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note, could the witness please be told to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They're really -- we need a clear record and it helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question with regard to your trip to the European Commission, do you recall whether you were successful in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had talks at various levels over there. We gave a presentation of our programme. Understandably, at the top-most levels we were told that we would receive assistance. There was no specific agreement. There was no specific document that was produced as a result of our request. There was nothing for us to sign. Nevertheless, within the framework of the regular assistance that was being shipped to Bosnia and Herzegovina by certain countries of the European Union, I'm sure that the document achieved some notable results nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01620, 1620. And it's dated 16 of August, 1992. This is a decision to implement the decree law on the currency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if you could take a look at that and I will be focussing primarily just on Articles 1, 2 and 3. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have an explanation? I'm not sure we're talking about the same document because the one that I have in front of me, the subject matter is the same, apparently. The date is the 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm looking -- I'm sorry, I'm looking at the very top of the page and you're looking at the end. But you're right, okay, it's 13th of August, 1992, at the very end. And my apologies. This is a decision to implement the decree law on the currency. Now, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please explain to us what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A while ago, we looked at a document by which the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Presidency adopted a decree law establishing the dinar as the official currency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was to be issued by the central national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was a decision that had to do with a principal, namely, it introduced a new currency into the monetary system of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a decision that talked specifically about a number of other things apart from the introduction of this new currency, it also comprised several other provisions, what the lower denominator would be, 100 para equals one dinar. It also introduced the designations for this new currency. Once the new currency was introduced, the old currency was no longer valid and then it talked about all the differences between the new currency and the old currency. Everything that was necessary for a currency to be able to viably function as a means of payment in a country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can see from Article 3 that on the day when this decision enters into force, that the new value shall be set for money issued by the national bank of Yugoslavia at the rate of 10 to 1. Why is that significant?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's significant because the money that had been in circulation up to this point in Bosnia and Herzegovina issued by the National Bank of Yugoslavia was devalued by inflation to a frightening extent. We had to make sure that we were on the safe side to the effect that the new currency would, be in a manner of speaking, more valuable. I'm not sure if that's of interest but I might as well explain that. This decision at the time assumed or rather it was based on the fact that the new currency that was printed would be brought into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to make sure that I understand this correctly so -- and I assume you're going to correct me if I am wrong because you've done that on several occasions so far so ...

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry but I have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's fine. And we strive for precision here. But up until this point in time, can we assume that there is no Bosnian currency, that they're using the old Yugoslav dinar, is that what the official currency was up until this period circulating in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document, 1D 0 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a follow-up question. In paragraph 3, it seems that former Yugoslav dinars will be replaced by Bosnian dinars at the ratio of 1 for 1 -- of 10 for 1, so 1.000 Yugoslav dinars are ten times less worth in Herceg -- Bosnia and Herzegovina dinars, is that how we're supposed to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to remind you that we're talking about the dinar and that was the official currency in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the ratio, you're quite right, Your Honour, that's 10:1. 1.000 dinars issued by the Yugoslav Central Bank will now be exchanged for 100 dinar issued by the Central National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wasn't that a blow to all people who owned Yugoslav dinars whose fortune was ten times less worth at once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is paper money, both. It's only worth whatever you can buy for it, therefore, this is no blow at all to those who expressed the value of their property in Yugoslav dinar because that currency no longer existed. It was as simple as that. There was now a new currency in circulation and the ratio was defined as 10 to 1. That was that. This is a technical reform that in no way changed or affected the value of the old currency. It is just that it is now expressed in a currency that is worth more in purely formal terms. How you choose to express this belongs to a very technical discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01622, 1622. This is a decision to put bank notes into circulation and withdraw bank notes from circulation. We see that this is 13th of August, 1992. Just focus on Article 1 and then I'll take you to Article 5, if you just look at those very briefly. In Article 1, it says, "On 17 August 1992, the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall put into circulation bank notes in denominations" and it lists them. And then going to paragraph number 5, it says, "The exchange of bank notes from item 2, paragraph 1 and 2 in this decision for bank notes from item 1 of this decision shall be carried out by the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the public auditing service of Bosnia and Herzegovina, banks and post offices with payment operations." Then it goes on to say that, "The exchange of bank notes for item 2, paragraph 2 of this decision shall take place solely in the area of the city of Sarajevo." Now, could you please explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is a document, it wasn't the government of the national bank of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Putting new bank notes into circulation is something that any central bank carries out. In this case, it's the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Article 1, it says what the actual bank notes will be and in number 2, it says when this will take place. I have to remind you of my statement in relation to money a few moments ago. All of this was done on the assumption that the money that was printed in Slovenia and that was transported or that was rather supposed to be transported to Sarajevo will in actual fact be brought into Sarajevo because Sarajevo was under a blockade. If you allow me, I'm just going to use three more sentences to explain the process. My task was to try to reach agreement with General McKenzie, the UNPROFOR commander that he make it possible for us to bring money into Sarajevo. We had a meeting and he promised that. There are two things that are very important from his promise that I wish to point out now. First of all, he promised that he would make it possible for us to have a plane land in Sarajevo, a plane that we would find. And secondly, the money that would be unloaded would be brought to the treasury of the central bank under a military escort. We found that to be satisfactory. However, two days later, I was informed by his people from his office, his staff, that this agreement was still in force except that he's adding two new ones. First of all, that the Serbs had to be informed what it was that was being transported; and secondly, that he cannot provide a military escort to us from the airport to the treasury of the national bank of Yugoslavia. That is when we decided not to try to bring money into Sarajevo anymore and this entire decision therefore practically lost not all of its importance but most of its importance. This was the truth and that is when we decided or rather later we decided to issue monetary coupons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to make sure I understand, General McKenzie was there on behalf of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of the UN forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought I'd point that out because there's been a lot of speculation about their contribution and we see one of them here. Now if we go on to 1D 01621. This is a decision to issue bank notes and the basic characterisation of bank notes. I just draw your attention to Article 5, I believe. Just as an example. Can you tell us what this is about, what this document -- and I suspect it's connected to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again this is a technical document that as a rule is adopted by the governor of the National Bank of Yugoslavia and what is specified here is what the bank notes would look like and generally speaking, all the other technical characteristics of the money involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us about not being able to bring in this money that had been printed in Slovenia. And incidentally, can you please tell us what the cost was, if you recall, I don't know if you mentioned that? Because I suspect that the Slovenians didn't do this out of the goodness of their hearts. This was not an altruistic act on their part?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order for the new money was one that was placed before I became a member of the government, the money was printed in Celje. If my memory serves me well and I hope that is the case, the price paid was 1.600.000 Deutschemark. When the money was printed and prepared for transport then upon orders from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in agreement with the government of the Republic of Croatia, this money was transported and stored in the treasury of the national bank of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01623. It's a very short document, we see it's 20 August 1992. I'll read the second paragraph under item one, it says, "On 20 August 1992, the national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall put into circulation monetary coupons in denominations of 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, 1.000, and 5.000 dinar as set out in the decision to issue monetary coupons and the basic characterisation of monetary coupons ..." and it gives a number. And then perhaps a more telling paragraph that I would like you to comment on, still under number one. "The monetary coupons mentioned in paragraph 2 of this decision shall be used as bank notes in the territory of the city of Sarajevo." So could you please comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that is a consequence of what I explained a few moments ago, namely, the fact that we could not transport the money that had been printed in Slovenia, we could not bring it into Sarajevo, and the money of the former Yugoslavia was no longer valid, the governor of the national bank passed a decision to print monetary coupons as surrogate money. I cannot fully comment on the second part of this decision why he decided that this would only be the case in the territory of Sarajevo. I assume, and this is just an assumption, Sarajevo was under blockade, probably this -- these coupons would have very little practical value on territories outside that environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you know for a fact whether these coupons, for instance, would have any value, say, in Zenica, based on this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me two sentences by way of an introduction because the subject matter is complex after all. Our idea was this real money that is also paper money but well, it looked differently, should be brought to Sarajevo or, rather, if it could not, then to Sarajevo, Livno, Duvno and other places. Since this was no longer a possibility then in the other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, people tried to make due in different ways. I personally know that coupons were printed in other areas as well. I know that proclamations were made to the effect that other currencies would be used as the currency like the German mark. Then other surrogates for the German mark and so on and so forth. So this is a situation and a time that gave rise to different solutions. All these monetary forms with the exception of real money like the German mark were practically very little value.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02695, 2695. This is a report on damage, transportation, infrastructure caused by the ravages of war. It's dated Sarajevo, 31 August 1992. This is Deputy Minister but we can't in English -- we haven't translated this can't recognise his signature. Do you recognise the name by any chance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Sarajevo. I did not see this document in Sarajevo, as far as I can remember, but I know how it came into being. I probably saw it later on in Zagreb. I know how these documents were created. The government then gave an instruction probably to assess war damages on basic infrastructure because, at that time, we harboured the illusion that the war would not last for a long time. In actual fact, we wanted to propose the establishment of an international aid fund for the development of Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international fund so we had to know what was damaged and to what degree in terms of infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the second sentence in the first page it says, "The transport infrastructure (tunnels, bridges, roads, rail roads, PTT," that's the postal service facilities and other "located on the axes of the aggressor's operations was a particular target of destruction." Do you know if this is correct, based on you living in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot confirm anything in specific terms but I assume this is correct because these are vital facilities for the functioning of life in general in a country and the economy in particular. There have to be these vital prerequisites for things to succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm mostly interested at this point because we will discuss it later on about the PTT services, the telecommunication services. At that point in time, can you please explain to us what the condition was in Sarajevo, especially with telecommunications and again I want you to link your answer, if it's possible, to the banking system, how it might affect banking transactions or commercial transactions in light of the system that was then operating or inherited prior to the -- to the war conditions.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that from the beginning of May that year, communications with the world were at first impeded and later on, they did not exist at all. I know that in terms of the communications that I could have then from the company that I worked in and later on from the government. I know that because I lived near the main post office building in Sarajevo that was the main communications centre with the foreign countries and I know that during the night between the 2nd and 3rd of May, and that is 150 metres away from my apartment, was -- this post office was totally destroyed. After that, communication became virtually impossible. We tried to make due in a different way. Energoinvest, my former company, bought a satellite telephone and through it we tried to communicate with the rest of the world. The government didn't have anything. Perhaps only a month after that, the prime minister brought in a telephone and the central bank after that brought in a third telecommunications set of this kind; so I think that was it. I can just say that communications in terms of all functions, that is to say, state organs, banks, companies, all of this was brought down to a very, very low level. Perhaps I should put it this way. It became impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to -- you indicated that the central bank received a telephone or a satellite telephone, that would have been in which month, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think sometime in the month of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I don't want to get ahead of myself but maybe this may be a good time because there is this organ or whatever you want to call it that is unknown to us, to many of us, called the payment bureau system. Could you tell us how that functioned briefly and how telecommunications might have been relevant with respect to the functioning of the payment bureau?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The payment bureau was the successor of the former public accounting service of Yugoslavia. Perhaps at that time it was still called the public accounting service. I assume that that was the case actually. Among other functions, as it's very name says, it was involved in payment operations between and among banks, companies, et cetera. All banks and companies had their own current accounts, giro accounts for carrying out their payment operations. Of course when the system of payments of a country functions, it is not physical money that is in circulation but information and when these -- this information is brought to a standstill, the system can no longer function. So very soon in the autumn of 1992, the system could no longer function. That is what had to do with internal payments. As for the other part of the story, that is to say, communication with the rest of the world, communication with external banks, technically, things were the same. Banks communicate between and amongst themselves by way of information that is transported through communications equipment and on that basis, payments are made and money is sold and purchased. If these communications do not work you cannot function, you cannot communicate, you cannot function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at next document 1D 02947 and this would tie in with your -- part of your, I think, a couple of answers ago when you talked about the establishment of an international fund for reconstruction and we see here -- and this is dated September 1992. And it document is entitled in fact, "The international fund for reconstruction development of the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And again, I believe we -- all we need to do is look at the very first page a little bit. The summary, that is. The first paragraph talks about roads, railway, the PTT communications having been destroyed. If we look at -- we skip one paragraph and we go on to the next, it says, "The Presidency and the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have initiated the concept of establishing the international fund for reconstruction and development of the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Then later, it lists after that, some priorities and if you go on to the third page, we see telecommunications being one of them, hence my previous question to you. Now, sir, could you please tell us a little bit about this. How was this document generated, if you know, and whether anything came about as a result of this concept of establishing an international fund for reconstruction and development?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again this has to do with part of the activities that are related to what we have already discussed and that is to say, the survival stuff. One of the conclusions from one of these meetings said that we decided to come up with this initiative to establish an international fund for assisting the development of Bosnia and Herzegovina and we started collecting money for that purpose. This document was prepared and it was adopted by the government and the Presidency, I assume. It was sent to about 10 different addressees in the leading countries in the world and Europe. Alija Izetbegovic spoke at the General Assembly of the United Nations in the second half of 1992 and he mentioned this idea in his expose, in his statement to the General Assembly. I, together with Mr. Ganic explained this idea in the European Union. There weren't any major results coming from that initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 01927. 1927. This is dated 1 September 1992. And I should point to Your Honours that with the exception of some chapters, I've tried to structure my direct in sort of a chronological order so we have a snapshot of history of how things progress. If you look at this document, this is 1 September 1992, if we look at the name at the bottom, it's Tomislav Krsticevic. You obviously know the gentleman; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Krsticevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we see that he's with the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a letter to the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Croatia and the very first sentence, we see it says, "As we are still unable to finance certain business trips abroad ourselves, we request that you once again render us a favour and pay to our professor Vladimir Trlin, the head of a team of experts for the succession of states, an advance of 10.000 Deutschemarks ..." and so on. Can you please explain to us why would it be necessary for a government official, a minister of transport and communications to be writing a letter to a ministry in Croatia, to the finance ministry to ask that Croatia pay for certain business trips being carried out by individuals from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as I've already said, Sarajevo was under a blockade. This was the 1st of September, 1992. Mr. Krsticevic was minister of trade and communications in the government and he sat in Zagreb. Mr. Trlin on the basis of the decision of the government represented Bosnia and Herzegovina in the expert group for succession of the former Yugoslavia and from time to time, this group would meet in Geneva, Brussels and elsewhere. Since Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have any resources, any money, any bank accounts, there was no way of paying this gentleman's expenses and for others, too, and the only way of dealing with this was to ask the Croatian government to handle this and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you say "that's what they did," the Croatian government provided the money for these trips.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian government on this occasion and later on on many occasions, and I can testify to that, did indeed lend that money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you go to the next document 1D 01558, 1558. This is dated Mostar, September 12th, 1992. It's addressed to the president of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the bottom we see it's from Dr. Jadranko Prlic, president of the HVO, HZ HB. And if you can just look at this document and I will be asking you a couple of questions in particular about the first three paragraphs or so. If you just look at this for a second. Now, it says here "Please find enclosed the acts passed by the temporary executive and administrative body Croatian Defence Council of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the period of imminent war, threat and in wartime with the aim to normalise life and activities of legal system in the liberated areas." It goes on to say, "In accordance with the decree of the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated May 2, 1992, certain legal regulations have been inherited from the former SFRY, while other regulations are declared null and void. By declaring those regulations null and void, a legal vacuum has been created, the consequences of which is the fact that the whole field, especially in economy, remained unregulated." It then goes on to say, "Since the daily life in the liberated areas required that these legal vacuums be filled, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was forced to pass regulations in these fields with the remark that all these regulations were passed as temporary regulations and they are limited to the period or war and imminent threat of war." My first question is and perhaps only question on this document because we'll have to take a break soon is: To your understanding, were there legal vacuums created as a result of what Dr. Jadranko Prlic is saying to the president of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina keeping in mind we're speaking of September 12, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just give a general answer to this. I'm not a lawyer but I do know that taking over regulations, because this was more or less the main task of the government at my time, taking over regulations from the former Yugoslavia and passing new regulations that were to be in force in wartime conditions and all of this led to many, many problems so I assume that what Mr. Prlic said in this respect is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's been translated as problems and it's my understanding that you said legal gaps. Is that correct? Are we talk being problems or gaps, legal gaps?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I did say that there were problems, different problems of different kinds because regulations either became dated or they were overcome or whatever, so in my view we can call all of this legal problems, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, I see the time. It may be good for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The registrar just told me that Mr. Karnavas has used up 1 hour and 57 minutes, so he still has 1 hour and 3 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at 1D 00036. If you don't have the document, I can provide it to you. 1D 00036. Do you have it, sir? Okay. Here, we see -- this is a decree on the regulation of payment transactions in Croatian dinars on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the immediate threat of war or state of war. We talked a little bit about the social accounting services. If we look at Article 2, it says, "Organisation units of the social accounting service (herein after the SDK) in HZ HB shall open a subgroup of accounts within the main group of accounts with numerical designation 1 written in the first column ..." and so on and so forth. Can you comment on this particular decree, sir, keeping in mind the time when it was issued, and this is 22 September 1992, and, of course, reminding us again the conditions and the importance of SDK, the social accounting services and how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand this decree as a technical decree on how a foreign currency should be used in the territory of Herceg-Bosna and in this case, Croatia's dinar. I don't see any essential elements in this decree that might suggest that the intention was to have Croatia's dinar as Herceg-Bosna's currency. There is nothing in it to suggest that the BH dinar should be abolished as a means of payment. I don't see here any intention to introduce the new currency. I don't see any suggestions here that all the values should be expressed in Croatia's dinar. I don't see any specific ratio being mentioned here. What this leads me to conclude is that this is a document of a purely technical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there is any questions from the Bench, I will go on to the next document. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question. This is a technical document, I therefore have technical question. Witness, you spoke about the exchange rate and you mentioned the fact that this decree does not aim to prohibit the use of BH -- the BH dinar because otherwise mention would have been made in that decree about the exchange rate. I know a long time has passed but could you tell us: What was the parity between the Croatian dinar and the BH dinar, was it a ratio of 1:1 or was it different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when the BH dinar was introduced. We did not establish its parity to any other currency. We started out with the assumption that the market would do its job in this respect and that market relations would then eventually establish the exchange rate and that's why it wasn't regulated there and I can't comment here either because it's not regulated here either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say that market relations established the exchange rate, that means there's a parallel market, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, by way of introduction, the exchange rate between two currencies can be fixed, this is something that is done by the central bank and then, for example, one assumes that a dollar is worth two units of another currency. And if the central bank maintains that rate, it becomes a fixed rate. You can do it differently, you can leave it to the market, the law of supply and demand to settle that and then the exchange rate is not a stable one, it fluctuates practically on a daily basis. We call this a floating exchange rate or a fluctuating exchange rate. Since we didn't have a fixed exchange rate in this case, obviously the intention was to leave this to the market and the law of supply and demand for that particular currency in the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps as a follow-up, why wasn't it fixed? Was that just a policy decision or was it a decision based on the realities of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat what I said a while ago. This decree did not define a number of other things either that would have led us to conclude that this currency was now being introduced as BH's official currency. None of the other elements are mentioned here. You don't have the exchange rate for that very reason. For that matter, there is no exchange rate defined for BH dinar and German mark, BH dinar and Croatia's dinar. This all depended on the supply and demand for that particular currency. Let me give you an example from Sarajevo, for example, the German mark was sometimes sold and exchanged for 100 Bosnian dinar. But sometimes it was a whole bag of BH dinars that you could get in exchange for a single German mark. It really very much depended on the fluctuations of the market day in, day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I go on to the next document 1D 02446, dated 26 September 1992. We see at the bottom that the gentleman's name is Hakija Turajlic, the deputy prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and he's also the chairman of the commission for weapons and military equipment. Of course along with this document there are other documents but first, if we could focus on the first page, it says, "On the basis of the agreement on friendship and cooperation with the Republic of Croatia dated 21 July 1992, items 8 and 10, it was decided that our states would initiate and develop cooperations on the manufacture and sale of weapons and military equipment." Then if we just go on to the next page, it talks about -- we see, "Our two republics jointly work on a few projects related to weapons and military equipment." I'm just reading the very first sentence. Page 3, the very top sentence, it says in the top paragraph, "This is a very significant task for the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as the job is very capital-intensive and requires significant capacity for key factories of the NVO, weapons and military equipment, industry in both republics." And I won't go through any other portions of the document. But first and foremost, I don't know if you told us, did you know Mr. Turajlic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Quite well, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And were you aware at all about this particular document, you know, the contents related in this document, that is, based on this friendship and cooperation agreement between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia here they want to initiate the development and cooperation in the manufacturing of weapons? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke several times within the framework of the government's so-called coordination for the economy and its various sectors and Mr. Turajlic was at the head of this initiative and the same applied to military cooperation or the development of military equipment in cooperation with Croatia therefore I'm familiar with that. As for the document itself, I didn't work on this document, however, I'm privy to the subject matter and if you want me to further elaborate on that, I'd be glad to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could, just with one or two more sentences, if you wanted supplement that.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 1980 and 1990, Yugoslavia produced tanks based on Soviet technology. Two types, T-72 and T-84. The tanks were sold abroad: Kuwait, Libya, a number of other countries like that. Industrial players from all over Yugoslavia were involved but the military production facilities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia were those most involved. The idea behind this was to try to pick up again this initiative and start again producing this tank, this was to be done in the Djuro Djakovic factory, the intention being for the military industries of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia to make up for those republican industries that on account of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia were now outside the production process and were no longer a player in that game.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02684 and this is a document that's addressed to the Croatian Defence Council Mostar. It's dated 17 October 1992. Again, we see Mr. Turajlic as the deputy prime minister and if we look at this document for a little bit, it says, "We have received your request" and it gives the number "of 5 October of this year referring to giving guarantees for an international loan of US $5 million." Then it goes on to say, "In order for us to be able to consider your request, we hereby ask you to inform us about the items [sic] of this loan. If you have a concrete offer (the foreign lender, the terms of payments, interests, et cetera)." "In your letter, you also mentioned sending us a bill of costs with basic items for financing the army but we have not received any, so we ask you to send it to us." "Kind regards." What can we draw, what conclusions can we draw from this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time but the way I understand this request, when the deputy prime minister Turajlic was writing this, he said that he needed this in order to be able to provide a guarantee for a foreign loan but for the government to be able to do that, he had to know the terms first for that loan and that I find to be perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this would have been the relationship between the government in Sarajevo, that is, him being -- acting on behalf of the government because he's deputy prime minister and the Croatian Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the deputy prime minister is here providing a reply to the Croatian Defence Council which had previously made a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And given his tasks as the deputy prime minister, would this have been within his remit?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the rules, in keeping with which the government was working this was something for the finance minister to reply to; however, I wasn't in Sarajevo at the time, I was in Zagreb. Why he took it upon himself to provide this response is not something that I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, and we're going to cover actually three documents with this but let's look at the next one which is 1D 02 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Karnavas. Before you enter into a different subject, I would like to ask a follow-up question. There is something which seems surprising. Witness, if I understand correctly, the HVO sent a letter on the 5th of October, unfortunately we do not have that letter because it would have been useful, and by this letter, the HVO asks the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to warrant a loan with somebody else, a loan of US $5 million. This letter which was sent by Mr. Turajlic seems to mention a loan concerning the financing of the army, meaning the HVO. From your point of view, in view of the fact that you held very high responsibilities as finance minister, does it mean that the level of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was not a refusal on the principle but the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was awaiting further information in order to warrant, if possible, that loan? Is this how we are supposed to understand this exchange, knowing that we do not have that letter dated 5th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind the general situation at the time, and the fact that we needed any assistance that we could get on any reasonable terms, and knowing that the HVO was viewed as a component of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and bearing in mind the nature of this response, I think the BH government would have provided a guarantee as long as the terms were acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something else that is not mentioned in this particular document but which is probably mentioned in the letter dated 5th of October. The HVO probably had contacts with a state entity, an individual state entity which was ready to loan those US $5 million provided that there was a warranty by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In financial terms, didn't that mean that the HVO was in contact with someone who was ready to provide this loan and this is quite a substantial amount of money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not familiar with these details. I didn't know about that at the time, but I would like to say this. It needn't have been the government. It could have been a bank or any other institution that wished to loan $5 million.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since we do not have that letter dated 5th of October, Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. If we go on to the next document, 2944, 2944.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see this is dated Mostar, 22 October 1992. At the very top, it's handwritten "Received at the office of BiH government on 23 October 1992, under number 05/1055." At the bottom, we see that this is from the Department of Finance head, Neven Tomic and this is about an overview of accounts of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. One, non-residential dinar account; two, non-residential foreign currency account; three, budget of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in BiH." Then there is an accompanying page with this and it has a breakdown of salaries, purchases of military equipment and so on. Can you please assist us, sir, because along with that there is also a document of -- it should be 16 October 1992, it's been -- it says September but if you look at the Croatian version, you will see that it actually says 23.10.1992. I'm sorry, it says -- if we look at Dr. Prlic's letter, we can see it there on the right-hand side. If you could look at these documents and please tell us what is in this bundle under what has been marked as 1D 02944 that was received by the office of BiH on 23 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first set of documents, there are two, three, four bills, invoices with certain amounts of money to be used for military purposes or equipment, military equipment and its value. This is something that was done by the company in Mostar that was producing aircraft and this was forwarded to the HVO. All the foreign -- the other document is something that talks about the breakdown of expenses but we don't know the exact period and we don't know exactly what it's about. I assume this is an assessment of Herceg-Bosna's financial needs over a certain period of time, that's the only reasonable conclusion that I can draw. The third document has the same nature as the first one. It is a request by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, President Pelivan for payments regarding military equipment. Again it was signed by Mr. Prlic. The fourth document is an attachment about the submission of invoices, those that I've been talking about, I assume. And there is another letter that I have here but it's a very poor copy and I really don't know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sticking with the letter that you indicated was to Jure Pelivan, if you could look at the date -- and this is from Dr. Jadranko Prlic to the president Jure Pelivan. Could you please -- are you able to make out the date?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as long as we are talking about the same document, I think so. Mostar, the 19th of October, 1992. This is a letter in which invoices are forwarded. The other letter that I said I couldn't read, that was illegible, what it comes across to me is the 20th of October, 1992, but it's quite illegible, therefore I'm not entirely certain what it says. I don't know that if that is what your question was about, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. And Your Honour, we have not translated what is under "Racun," which are the receipts and we will do so at some point but due to time considerations we were unable to do that.
