Can you explain to us why would these matters be sent to the government by Mr. Tomic and by Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the explanation is simple. They were asking to be paid, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in addition, they provided the accounts to which the money was supposed to be paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 02948, we see your name at the bottom of this document. We see that it's dated 11 November 1992, and it says, "Pursuant to the arrangement made between Mr. Primorac and Mr. Martinovic, please make the following payments to our accounts." First, who is Mr. Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, at the time, was an advisor to the director-general of Privredna Banka Zagreb and before that he was the minister of finance for the Republic of Croatia. Since our financial relations, that is to say, those between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia primarily went through this bank, Privredna Banka Zagreb, the operative person who was in charge of these relations was the gentleman concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us what exactly is this document about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have explained, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a policy of helping Bosnia and Herzegovina whenever possible, whenever they had the necessary financial resources. In this document, I request that Privredna Banka to pay 1 million Deutschemark to Herceg-Bosna as soon as possible, also to make a payment to the municipality of Orasje, 100.000 marks, again through Herceg-Bosna, to ensure for our office in Zagreb 50.000 Deutschemark and to provide us with 30.000 Deutschemarks in cash in order to cover the expenses of our delegations going to meetings in Geneva, devoted to the succession of the former Yugoslavia and so on. So it is through this channel that I am trying to do what I can with Mr. Turajlic, who was my contact person in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could help us out a little bit. We know where Herceg-Bosna Mostar is -- but Orasje municipality, do you know offhand where that would be?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. I do know full well because I'm from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Orasje is at the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Sava River, that is to say, the northern-most part on the other side of the Sava River is the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is that region called anything, does it come by a particular name?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That area, is it called -- is it ever referred to by another name?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area not only of the municipality of Orasje, but also of the neighbouring municipalities is usually referred to as "Posavina".

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I know it but others may not. But thank you for that clarification. All right. If we go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, a very short follow-up question. This document shows that on the 11th of November, 1992, you as the minister for finances of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina asked the Privredna Banka of Zagreb to transfer to Herceg-Bosna Mostar 1 million Deutschemarks. When you sent this request, I suppose you had the agreement of the prime minister of the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is a biggish amount, I had Mr. Turajlic's consent at the time because usual practice in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was that Mr. Turajlic and I sign everything that has to do with military expenses. I as Minister of Finance and he in his capacity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the budgetary and financial aspects of this, because this involves or has an effect on the finances of Bosnia and Herzegovina because at least 1 million would be given to Herceg-Bosna, did you need to have a prior political agreement? Would this type of decision have the agreement of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of its president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so because it has to do with the budget of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that was adopted already around the middle of the year, as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm thinking in political terms. You're part of a government that carries out a specific policy as defined by the prime minister but there's also a Presidency that may have a say and it may be that Mr. Izetbegovic would not be in agreement either. Therefore, such a commitment for a sizeable amount, did it need the political agreement of the highest level, for instance, by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to whether this kind of political agreement had to exist, probably the prime minister would have to know about that. The next document will show that he was aware of what I say asking for because he also issues an order to Mr. Krsticevic who was a signatory of our account to transfer 1 million DM to Herceg-Bosna; so these two documents are complementary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at 1D 02943 and I believe this is the document that you were referring to and I guess this goes back to what you had told us earlier when you said that Bosnia and Herzegovina would help Herceg-Bosna and can you please assist us with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the number, it was very fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D 023943 is the number, is that what we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] This is an order issued by Prime Minister Pelivan and it consists of two matters. First of all, why is he addressing Krsticevic and not me? I am the minister of finance but he is addressing Krsticevic here who is also a member of the government and who was a signatory of the resident account of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Opuzen. At that time I was not a signatory and that is why this was sent to Krsticevic. It consists of two things. One is to stop paying all money orders from this account in Ploce and Opuzen except for 1 million Deutschemark remittances to the HVO. So Herceg-Bosna or, rather, HVO was remitted 1 million Deutschemarks and the stoppage of other payments is a consequence of the fact that we decided to restructure the orders or, rather, all the accounts held in Croatian banks and that will be shown by the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I believe the next document you are speaking of is 1D 02690.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the approval of the prime minister, I decided that we should close down all non-resident accounts that had existed until then and that our future financial operations, that is to say, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia should be organised through three accounts in Zagreb. One account was for the office of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina for current expenses. This account would have Krsticevic and Goluza as the officers authorised to sign transactions. The second account would be for humanitarian aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina. This would be signed by Amila Omersaftic and Minister Raguz, the lady was head of the government office for humanitarian aid. And the third account of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be signed by myself, Zarko Primorac; Tomislav Krsticevic, who was minister of trade; Goluza, Josip, who was deputy minister of trade; and Logo, Muhamed, who was my deputy. So financial operations in the Republic of Croatia were fully stabilized in this way and were fully transparent too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The documents we have just been going through is 1D 02690 followed by 1D 02691 and 1D 02692; is that correct? That's what you just -- these are the documents that you were referring to in your previous answer?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the documents that we were -- that I was discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this might be a good time for us to ask you and for you to discuss -- you know, you indicated that you weren't in Sarajevo and so could you please tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Document 1D 02692, the third one, Witness, I can see that you now have the signature because we can see your name in this document. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So had you decided that you could, of your own accord, withdraw or give orders without having to go through Krsticevic or Goluza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A document is missing here, one that I compiled at the time in Zagreb and in this document, I prescribed how financial operations would take place in Croatia, those of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean. This document precisely described how these operations would take place, cash operations, how documentation was to be filed, and stored and so on. Within this programme of putting into order the financial operations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia, there were these documents, too, that created a system of non-resident accounts in Croatia and they were made fully transparent in this way. This was solely my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could please explain to us, you were in Zagreb at the time and I know we've heard a little bit of testimony in this courtroom about that but could you please tell us where were you working out of Zagreb and why were you not in Sarajevo because this is a period when you are the Minister of Finance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of a decision of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I left Sarajevo on the 18th of September, 1992, as head of a delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was supposed to take part in the work of the annual assembly of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Washington in the second half of 1992. In addition to myself, there was Mr. Andrijic, the governor of the central bank, he was also on this delegation, and in Washington, the delegation was joined by the then ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Mr. Mihat Brankovic, who was the representative of Energoinvest in Washington. They were also appointed members of the delegation. Upon my return, as you saw in the government programme, I was supposed to work on the integration of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the European Bank of Reconstruction and Development, also to sum up work in terms of succession of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also to work on the establishment of a bank for Bosnia and Herzegovina in Vienna. There were also many other obligations that were of an international nature. I could not do that kind of work from Sarajevo. No one could have done that work from Sarajevo because quite simply there was a communication blockade. That is to say that I spent about a month and a half doing this kind of work in Zagreb. When I brought this work to a level that I considered that something had been achieved, I returned to Sarajevo and together with Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Andrijic, I was supposed to fly on an UNPROFOR flight to Sarajevo. It could have been the last days of November. On that same day when I was supposed to take this flight in the afternoon, I received information from Mr. Turajlic, Pelivan and Andrijic are witnesses to that, that I should not return then, rather, that I was supposed to wait for Ganic to get out of Sarajevo so that we could go together to the European Union to present our programme for the survival of the population. I waited for Ganic. A few days later he got out of Sarajevo. We went to Brussels and Geneva together. We presented this programme and I returned to Zagreb, say, sometime towards the end of the first part of the month of December. That is when I was informed that the government was being reconstructed. Since I did not wish to be a member of the government anymore, it seemed pointless for me to go back at that point in time. Once again, may I repeat, I did not leave Sarajevo, I worked upon instructions. I had intended to return. I was registered as a person who was to be returned but this was delayed due to the circumstances involved. There is another thing I would like to mention, perhaps it's not important but already at that time, my apartment in Sarajevo had already been destroyed and, for all intents and purposes, I had nowhere to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just two very quick documents for housekeeping purposes. 1D 01630. This is dated 10 November 1992 and it's a decision, it says "To accept the resignation of Jure Pelivan," I believe that was the prime minister under which you were working, or the president of the government. It says here prime minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then of course the next document, 1D 01408. This is -- this refers to the election of Mr. Akmadzic replacing Mr. Pelivan; correct? To your knowledge, that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't down there but this is what happened, according to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And there was a period of time when you were -- well, we know that you worked for -- under Prime Minister Jure Pelivan and it's my understanding that there was some time that you also worked under the new Prime Minister Akmadzic; is that correct? Or do I have it wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at the next document, 1D 02693, 2963. This is November 20th, 1992. Again, this may have -- may be linked to your previous answer concerning why you were not in Sarajevo to some extent and we'll see how. This is a request for issuing a certificate on meeting the conditions of the registration of LT/Livno-Tomislavgrad Trading Bank DD Livno." And we can see here, it says that "Since 28 December 1989, the Livno main branch office has been working as part of the Sarajevo Commercial Bank DD without the status of a legal entity." Now, if we skip down a couple of paragraphs, it then goes on to say, "With the breakout of the war in the RBH, Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, communication between the Livno main branch office and the head office was completely cut off. However, in spite of the absence of communications, the Livno main branch office continued to work in the conditions of an imminent threat of war." Then if we look at the rest of the document, we see what their request is. Can you please help us out here. What exactly is being sought through this letter? Because you already told us previously that the communications were not functioning in Sarajevo. And again remind us how that might have been important with this Livno branch at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, or up until that time, up until the war broke out, Privredna Banka Sarajevo was in existence as a central headquarters and within it there were several branch offices including the one in Livno. As for the distribution of work within the bank, it was such that foreign currency transactions, that is to say, relations with foreign countries, payments, international credits and so on and so forth all of that was work that was done by headquarters on behalf of their branch offices. In other words, let me link all of this up to this document. When the communications blockade of Sarajevo and the headquarters of this bank was in force, the branch offices could no longer carry out foreign transactions. First of all, they didn't have the authorisation. Secondly, they didn't have the communication needed in order to continue foreign transactions, at least as far as I was concerned, and -- that is to say, the payments of pensions of our workers who had worked in Germany and had payments, on account of that pensions, our branch office in Livno and elsewhere had to do something about this to reestablish communication either to reorganise themselves, to become independent, or to find a third way. According to this document, this branch office decided to become independent and this is what I can infer on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would you say, and I don't want to lead you but would you say this is one of the consequences of the disruption of the communications and -- what the war brought out?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely that is one of the consequences of this war. Had there not been a war, this would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 1D 02698. This is dated 20 November 1992. We see Mr. Turajlic again. And we see the subject here is the platform for the talks of the delegation of the RBH at the seat of the EC. Attached to it is the platform and if we look on the third page, under item number 4, we see the international fund for the reconstruction of RBH. Now, to save time, it would appear that here, this is in of what you've already told us about of your participation and Mr. Turajlic's and others in putting a platform together for the survival of the population and having discussions with the EC and the intention to establish an international fund for reconstruction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct. I was always very specific about these talks. This is the platform that was used by Mr. Ganic and myself. This is a platform that was established by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina both Mr. Ganic and I used it in our negotiations with our negotiations -- within our negotiations with the European Union towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to have to caution you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. [Interpretation] Was I speaking too fast again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 02949. And we only translated a portion of this but if we look at it from the very top, we see your name. We see that it's addressed to the president of the government, Mr. Akmadzic, and if you look at -- under item 5 which was translated and we'll have the rest of the document translated, Your Honours, but again this is one of the documents we received rather late. It says here, "Pensions in foreign currencies" and again this is linked up to what you told us already. You say, "Pensions in foreign currencies and assistance to our citizens from Germany and other countries have not been paid since April this year. The money is at German banks around 4 million Deutschemark. This problem is especially pronounced in western Herzegovina and Central Bosnia." Then you say, "To solve this problem, it would be necessary that the following persons get out of Sarajevo: Responsible manager of Privredna Banka Sarajevo and director of PIO BiH Luka Sijalkovic [phoen]." And can you please tell us why was it necessary for you to send this letter to Mr. Akmadzic, the president of the government and why were you asking that these individuals leave Sarajevo just -- I want to hammer home this point?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a situation in which the pensions earned by BH citizens in Germany were available for transfer to Bosnia and Herzegovina and for distribution to pensioners who were now resident in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the communication lines broke down and these funds accumulated in German banks and could not be transferred to Bosnia. There were problems in other sectors too and the remaining portion of the document will show that. I sought a solution and one of the solutions was for someone who was responsible on behalf of the Privredna Banka to come out. I wrote to the prime minister to familiarise him with the problem and to ask for his assistance to leave Sarajevo. I'm just telling you this to illustrate what the situation was. None of the managers of any bank or any institution could leave unless previously authorised by the prime minister or the president of the Presidency. Therefore, this was addressed to the prime minister. We had to look for a solution and that is the gist of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The very last sentence or paragraph, you say, "There are similar problems related to the collection of Iraqi debts which are considerable for us. I have taken measures so that some people get out and go to Geneva, but your support is needed here as especially regards the bank and retirement insurance." So this again supports what you just told us, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but if I may just say a word or two about the Iraqi debt. The UN set up a special committee to deal with Iraqi debt after the first Iraqi war back in 1991. B & H according to our records, or rather, companies from B & H were making claims worth millions of dollars from Iraq. It was very important for someone who understood the problem to leave Sarajevo, to go to Geneva and try to deal with it. That is why I pointed out about those people leaving that were dealing with this Iraqi business and then people who were dealing with the pension funds and people who -- the pension funds and the bank as soon as possible for those people to leave Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 02942, 2942. We see your name at the top of this document and as I understand it, you even provided it to us. If we go at the last page in the original version, we see that it's dated December 8, 1992. And this is information on the financial dealings of the government of BiH in Zagreb, of the government of the government in BiH in Zagreb. That's what it says. Then you talk about the relations with Privredna Banka. If we could just look at this first page under information and tell us what is this about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you remember, we spoke yesterday in the morning or earlier about the so-called advance payment granted by the Croat government to Bosnia and Herzegovina. That had now been exhausted and we needed new funds for all sorts of purposes. So first I got into negotiations with the finance ministry of the Republic of Croatia and they granted their approval as a matter of principle for a new loan from Croatia. This time around, we asked for a billion and a half dinar and a million dollars and this would be distributed in different ways. There were negotiations with the Privredna bank and the government and then I informed the prime minister and that's how far the whole matter got. Otherwise, the date on this is the 8th of December which is exactly the time I came back from Brussels and I probably already decided that I would not be part of this new government which had already been reconstructed. And this is one of the documents in which I am informing everybody else as to what I've been doing and what was still open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, of particular importance and the Trial Chamber may want some clarification is where you say here, "The contract with the bank has not been signed yet. The bank has firmly promised to approve the loan. Until now, the following financial means for these accounts have been engaged" and then you say "For Herceg-Bosna Mostar in accordance with the government's conclusion, the value of 1 million Deutschemarks and dinars." Now, we saw some earlier documents. Is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two figures are linked to what we've been saying but there's a new element here. At the time, we received a substantial amount of humanitarian aid from England, its value being, as far as I remember, about 9 million German mark. However, we needed 216.000 pounds to secure the -- to cover the shipment fees and the storage fees. We didn't have that kind of money and we had to go back to the Croatian government to help us with that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And of course we could see on this very same page where you do discuss or inform everybody about the opening of non-residential accounts and that was based on what we have already seen; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is related to what I was speaking about earlier, the opening of new non-residential accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. If we look at 1D 02682, 2682, this is 2 December 1992. This is addressed to the mission of the RBH government, personally to Tomislav Krsticevic and we see at the bottom it's signed by HZ HB vice-president a Mr. Ivankovic. The very first paragraph says, "The Croatian Defence Council has organised a defence war in the territory of Bosnian Posavina and has been conducting it from its very beginning without any help from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is why we now ask you, for the first time, to help us financially at a critical [sic] moment for us and thus enable us to overcome the problem of financing our formations which has been critical for a long time already." And we see the amount that they are being asked. Do you know anything about this particular request of 2 December 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was received by the government's office in Zagreb on the 15th of December, 1992. As this shows, this was just before the reconstruction of the government. Therefore, I'm not familiar with this document but there is one other thing that I have to say and I have to remind you that we looked at other documents and it was clear that we had issued an order to the Privredna Bank to use some of our funds and to pay 100.000 German marks to Orasje municipality from those accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's why I asked you about Posavina so we could tie it up together. All right. Very nicely. 1D 02683. 1D 02683. We see your name at the bottom. This is 11 December 1992. Here, again, we saw an earlier such document. This is addressed to a commercial bank in Zagreb and you're saying -- at the top, we see Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina government, Ministry of Finance. "We hereby ask you to pay the amounts given below to members of the succession group delegates of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the ICFY in Geneva who are travelling to Geneva on 12 December 1992 ..." what is this document about, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another document of this kind. There were members of the BH commission that went to the succession talks in Geneva. Some of those members of that group were in Sarajevo or were from Sarajevo. Mr. Trlin, for example, was in Zagreb at the time, but as a rule, these members did not have sufficient funds to cover their travel expenses. Whenever a situation like this occurred, we would go to the Privredna bank in Zagreb the same bank whose services we used for our other transactions and we would ask them to cover the travel expenses incurred by those members, obviously, that would later be charged to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02681. Again we see your name. This is dated 17 December 1992, and this says "We hereby ask you to transfer 20 million Croatian dinars from the non-residential account of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to this particular -- to the account of the office of the RBH government at the Commercial Bank Zagreb." This -- again we have your name. Can you please explain what this document is about and what it illustrates. That's probably the perhaps most important aspect is what does this illustrate so we have a good sense, so we don't draw any wrong conclusions of what is a non-residential account and who should have one and if there are any sinister motives behind opening such an account.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain yesterday why these non-residential accounts were necessary and why the non-residential accounts were not only functioning between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia but were also beginning to function in relation to the other republics as well. If there are any more detailed questions about this, please ask them but all means but speaking of this document, it should be simple enough to explain. Quite simply, I'm applying to a bank that still has a non-residential account to transfer to Zagreb 20 million Croatian dinars which didn't strike anyone as a large sum of money at the time. It was actually quite negligible, believe me, at the time to cover the expenses of the BH office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 01931. This is dated 26 December 1992. We see at the bottom it's vice-president of the government, Mr. Turajlic, and if you look under item number 1, it says "Zarko Primorac is hereby authorised to run the operational side of the loan and, in contact with the Privredna Banka Zagreb, prepare and initial the text of the loan contract." Of course we can see above that about certain conclusions of the government concerning $1 million. Could you please explain to us what exactly Mr. Turajlic is asking of you or authorising you to do, keeping in mind that this is 26 December 1992, and I think that you either have resigned by this point or are rapidly coming upon your resignation?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've looked at that document showing that in keeping with a conclusion by the BH government, I had applied to Croatia to give us an additional loan, 1 billion and a half Croatian dinars and 1 million dollars which is something that should have been dealt with through the Privredna bank as anything else that we were doing with Croatia. These negotiations were in progress when I was relieved of my duties, which was on the 21st of December, 1992. The document was written on the 26th and Mr. Turajlic authorised me to continue in an operative sense to see the deal through, for the contract to be signed, but the contract was eventually signed by the appropriate minister in the BH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 01930, dated 15 January 1993. We see Mr. Akmadzic's name as the president of the government and it says here, "Pursuant to the conclusions adopted by the government at its 104th session held on 20 December 1992," we saw that earlier in the previous document, he goes on to say, "I hereby authorise Mr. Martin Raguz, minister of labour and social welfare, to sign the contract with Privredna Banka Zagreb." So in the previous document we saw that you were run to operational side, initialling it, I guess, at some point, and here it would appear here that Mr. Raguz is going to be signing the contract. Can you explain that to us so we can understand it? What's going on?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is perfectly simple. In my capacity as minister, I started those negotiations but when I was about to leave, the negotiations had not yet reached a conclusion. Mr. Raguz was not a financial expert. I don't remember what it was that it was called that he did but he did something different altogether. He couldn't go on with these negotiations because they were of a technical nature so the government decided that despite the fact that I was no longer minister I should see the deal through. That I should hash out the terms of the agreement and the contract with the Croatian government and that he, as officially the minister, a minister in the BH government should be the one to sign the contract. Mr. Raguz as officially a minister with the BH government to sign the contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So from that, I mean I guess we can conclude that Mr. Turajlic at least had confidence in you to allow to you continue with this particular task, that is getting the loan even after you had -- you were no longer the minister.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope so. It didn't matter but I had been working with Mr. Turajlic for 25 years, that's one thing you should keep in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And that was the gentleman incidentally that unfortunately and regrettably was killed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is a gentleman who was killed in an UNPROFOR vehicle in Sarajevo. UNPROFOR, the -- were taking back from Sarajevo airport to the centre of town. The vehicle was intercepted. The UNPROFOR soldiers opened the vehicle, I'm not sure what the circumstances were surrounding this, but eventually he was killed inside that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go to the next document, 1D 01584, if we look at this document, it says, "Report on the activities of the RBH government logistics centres for humanitarian aid in the Republic of Croatia from 1 January 1993 to 31 May 1993." Obviously this is after you have left. We do see on top two names, Josip Goluza and Zlatko Hurtic. And of course if you look at the third paragraph of this document on the first page, it says, "The logistics centres, however, had been operating even prior to that," to a date being referenced in February 20th, 1993, "for instance, one in Ploce since June 1992 and one in Split since July 1992. Their operations were, however, quite uncoordinated in terms of both reception and distribution of incoming aid." And I point that out just to make reference that this would have been the period when you were a minister with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about paragraph 3 on page 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was a foundational question because my next question was going to be -- well, first, obviously you know these two gentlemen; correct? One is a Croat and the other one is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I know Goluza quite well. I know Hurtic a little less well, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were they both located in Croatia at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both because Goluza, as far as I know, the government appointed Goluza deputy trade minister. That was Jure Pelivan's government, that was probably extended. He had been nominated by the government to be in charge of this humanitarian aid business and to be in Zagreb. He ran the whole thing and he was the head of the Zagreb office. Hurtic was a different thing altogether. He had been tasked by the government to deal with refugees, people who were on the fringe of society, humanitarian aid, and so on and so forth and he had a job in the Zagreb office but his job was different from that of Mr. Goluza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just one technical question -- before I get to that question. This document here and the data that is included in here, would this be the sort of data that you have come across while you were Minister of Finance with respect to activities resulting from these logistics centres?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to understand your question better. Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see a lot of data here and obviously you were in Zagreb at one point as the Minister of Finance and I'm wondering whether during your tenure, obviously you must have known that there were logistics centres and I'm just wondering whether the data that we see here is the sort of data that was being collected for accountancy and transparency purposes that you would have been aware of at the time when you were serving?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I can't say whether it was done this systematically but my involvement with this part of the government's activity was about this whenever funds were needed to ship aid, to store aid, other types of financial services too. Knowing Mr. Goluza, who is a very serious individual, I think whenever there was an operation -- and that part of service that he was in charge of -- well, you know, that he absolutely -- I think one might even say he -- and I can sort of link this up with what I said before. This was entirely transparent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said knowing Mr. Goluza who was a very serious individual in the way he went about his job, I'm almost certain that whenever there was an operation that was his responsibility, he recorded this in the appropriate way and then he went on to inform the government of BH about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are two or three minutes beyond schedule. I don't know what the other Defence counsel intend to do. I don't know whether there will be cross-examination. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have three documents -- well, two to three documents left and I think I can wrap it up in five minutes, Your Honour. And I had initially predicted four hours. I don't know about my colleagues. I'm told there may be another five minutes or ten minutes from them but I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one housekeeping matter because I failed to ask this question. At this time when you have this office that you are operating out of that is for Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, was there another office for other matters such as -- that would serve as a diplomatic mission as it were or had the embassy already been opened?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Zagreb, I found this office of which Mr. Goluza was head, as I said. This office mostly dealt with issues to do with humanitarian aid, the transit of goods, that sort of thing, generally speaking. I was never a member of that office. I simply worked there for a while. I would go there because I had nowhere else to work. As for everything else, I know that sometime in mid-July, the Presidency appointed Mr. -- Mr. -- the name escapes me but I'll tell you the gist of the matter and then maybe we can trace the name. An office was set up that dealt with the diplomatic -- issues of diplomacy and consular business. Another gentleman was appointed head who taught at the faculty of economics in Zagreb and he's even a member of the Croatian parliament, Dr. Semso Tankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you just tell us that name again because it's not in the record.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Semso Tankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now just very quickly, 1D 01928, this is a document and again this is for the purposes of -- that we can see a snapshot in history. Now we're in 1 June 1993, and this is from Governor Stiepo Andrijic, we know that he is the governor of the national bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and this is in regards to a loan, a rather small loan, I guess, by those days, 100.000 Deutschemarks. And he says, "I refer to my conversation with Mr. Josip Martinovic during which I attempted to convey the need of the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a short-term loan in the amount of 100.000 Deutschemark." Now, Martinovic, again, if you could help us out, who was he, and why would the governor of the National Bank be asking this gentleman for a loan presumably for the National Bank?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me remind you, allow me, I said before that, the Privredna Banka Zagreb was a bank that was authorised to handle many transactions of this kind with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Martinovic, at the time, was an advisor to the general director of the Privredna Banka in Zagreb and before that, he was the finance minister for the Republic of Croatia. So this document shows another thing. At all times, not just me as a minister but also other institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I'm talking about the national bank and everybody else, whenever we are facing a national difficulty and at the time we were facing a great deal of financial difficulty -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down, you're almost there.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me, in my capacity as the finance minister, and other institutions of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina including the central bank whenever we were facing some sort of financial difficulty or whenever there was a shortage of cash which was a recurring situation at the time, we would always use this channel to address the Croatian government and ask them for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We can see that in 1D 01929, this is from Mr. Goluza, this is 3 June 1993, where he's asking for the payment of travel expenses nonetheless incurred by our government officials. Is that correct? This is another example?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another example but let me just add one more thing. This is a document according to which Mr. Krsticevic and I are settling final financial accounts with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have one last document and this will take about 30 seconds. Again, now we are in -- this is January 1993. We have could have handled this a little earlier but I just want to focus your attention on this, this document here. As of 25 January 1993, we have the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They're putting into circulation money coupons and now it's in denominations of 5.000 and 10.000 dinars. So do you know whether, as of January 25, 1993, whether Bosnia and Herzegovina had a currency that was not of this type that you could circulate the news throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina? Because here we're talking about coupons and we saw earlier the coupons were referring to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, can you give us the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 15th January, 1993, decision to put into circulation money coupons. So we see here it's January 25 that the National Bank is going to be putting out in circulation more coupons. And my question was and we saw that earlier the coupons were for Sarajevo only, do you know whether there was any hard currency that could be used, that was being generated, that is, by Bosnia and Herzegovina that could be used throughout the free territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time and perhaps even outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina as hard currency?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, may I answer the question that has to do with the bank notes and then I'm going to add something that is of relevance to the entire area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Although this is the period when I was not -- no longer in the government, I assume that this is a decision putting into circulation coupons that were of higher value. Obviously, inflation had taken its toll and it was necessary to introduce coupons of a higher value in order to reduce the amount of paper involved. The second question, whether there was a currency that was valid throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina formally, yes, it was the dinar issued by the National Bank or, rather, issued by the central bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This decision was passed in the month of August. In essence, this was a situation that cannot be described simply. There was not a single currency that prevailed physically throughout the area. In Sarajevo, there was these coupons. Other municipalities had issued their own coupons, I will have to check the dates but I think that the districts of Zenica and Tuzla had already introduced the German mark as their currency so there was this great deal of variety throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Primorac, I want to thank you very, very much for answering my questions and I trust you will answer any other questions with equal clarity no matter where they come from in this courtroom. Thank you very, very much. Your Honours, I have no further direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to have a break. I think it's best to break now. And we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Let me ask the Defence teams. 2D?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful. On behalf of Bruno Stojic, we have no questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Praljak's Defence will just have a few questions, just a few minutes, but my colleague Ms. Tomasegovic would be in the right order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Petkovic will have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will say briefly what it is that I would like to put questions about. It will have to do with the transactions of Energoinvest on the very eve of the war, that is to say, the late 1980s and the early 1990s. The witness said what his position was during the direct examination and he spoke briefly of the Energoinvest company; however, if the Trial Chamber believes that I go beyond the direct examination in my questions, I understand that the time would then be taken away from the overall time given to the 5D Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, ask your questions since the witness said that he worked in that company and I myself had wondered as to the importance and the part played by this company in the general economy. So please go ahead. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Also, by your leave, I have two documents that I do not wish to tender through this witness, however, I have prepared them for the sole reason of showing them to the witness in order to jog his memory so that we could move on more quickly. This is an economic project 20 years ago so I would just like to remind him of what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, I am Dijana Tomasegovic-Tomic attorney-at-law from Zagreb and I act as Defence counsel for Mr. Valentin Coric in these proceedings. Since I see that both you and I seem to be fast speakers, I will kindly ask you to ask you to listen to the interpretation and when you hear that it is over, only then start giving an answer. So please give a brief pause between my question and your answer. Mr. Primorac, you told us that in the 1980s, you were the vice-president of the business board of Energoinvest; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you remember or, rather, do you know how many people were employed by Energoinvest at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period when Energoinvest was in full swing, I can say between 1980 and 1985, the maximum number of employees was 55.000. After that, some of the organisations separated from Energoinvest. If I understand you correctly, you are referring to 1989 and 1990. I don't know the exact figure for that period but I assume that it was about 50.000 employees.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Energoinvest had a market throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia and I assume that it was also involved in exports outside the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Energoinvest had companies or factories throughout the former Yugoslavia, all the republics of the former Yugoslavia. I stand corrected. This happened when the company was in full swing. Later on, some of these companies separated from Energoinvest. As for exports, it was the biggest exporter of the former Yugoslavia. Energoinvest exported to about 30 countries throughout the world. These exports amounted to $800 million per year in the years of our greatest activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Since this was in the time of Yugoslavia and since this was such a big company, it was only natural that this company employed persons of all ethnic backgrounds, that Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks were employed and all the others in the company; right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, no one paid any attention to that, to how many persons from what ethnic background were employed in the company. It was only natural that persons of all ethnic backgrounds were employed there so that question was totally irrelevant while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, Aluminij Mostar, was this an organisation that was within Energoinvest in 1987?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just say two things before giving a direct answer? Energoinvest built Aluminij Mostar. The first contract with Pechiney, a French company, was signed in 1969. The Alumina factory was commissioned in 1975, the electrolysis factory Elektroliza Mostar, the best-known company, was commissioned in 1981. After that, Aluminijumski Kombinat Mostar separated from Energoinvest but I think that was in 1989.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I put the question, could the usher please give the witness these documents so that he can have a look at them so that ... Witness, our usher will now give you two documents. One document pertains to the project of the factory in Citluk and the other document is an opinion of the chamber of commerce of Bosnia and Herzegovina about this same project. Now I'm going to ask you whether you remember that in 1987, this project was developed within the programme of the Citluk factory. We see here that the author of the project is the work organisation Energoinvest Aluminij Mostar and that within this project in addition to this factory, yet another factory was supposed to be built in Ljubusko?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just continue along what you were saying. You were right in 1987, that was the case and it is shown that by these documents. Our policy was, in our company, to build as many processing facilities as possible throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina with the objective of having primary aluminium that was produced in Mostar processed throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is better than exporting raw aluminium. Several different facilities were built for that purpose throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, I can tell you what they were if necessary. I was not directly involved in this line of work at the time but I think that this was a programme that implied that a new factory would be built in Citluk and I think that this was a topical programme but the factory was not built.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember the protagonists of these project, do you remember -- it's on the next page, Zarko Bilic, Radoslav Krkelic [phoen], Sadik Dizdarevic, Valentin Coric, Milan Jovicic, do you remember talking to these persons and cooperating with them on this project?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know more or less all of these persons. This is the director of the secretary of development of the aluminium complex in Mostar, that is to say, the sector that was supposed to develop then. It was Sadik Dizdarevic, if I remember correctly, he is referred to here as the protagonist or the -- I don't know exactly what his position was. But the director of the OOUR in Citluk was Zarko Bilic, also a person I know well, Valentin Coric too, so all the persons mentioned here I think they were in a way involved in this project.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the basis of this opinion of the chamber of commerce of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the metallurgy association from 1987, their opinion about this project. This is the opinion on the harmonization of this programme with the policy of development established by the social plan of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period from 1986 until 1990. What I'm interested in in relation to this opinion, is the following: When I look at the opinion and the project, it seems to me, I'm a layman, I'm not a economist, I'm not a business woman, I don't know much about this but it seemed to me that this was a big investment, a meaningful investment that would be important for the economic development of the area where the factories would be built in terms of employing people, making money and so on. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, definitely. As soon as the project was the subject of harmonization within the chamber of commerce of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it had to be a meaningful project. I don't know what its actual size was but since it had to undergo this procedure, it certainly had to be a significant project.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMESAGOVIC-TOMIC
utterances.text: My last question. Tell me, please, Energoinvest, this is a hypothetical question, actually that I'm going to put but you were on the board, you held one of these top positions so I'm sure that you will be able to answer. I'm referring to Energoinvest and the investors and the protagonists of this project. If anyone knew that there could be a war or had planned a war, would they go for such a project and in that case, would they plan to build this kind of factory because this is not a one-year project that would simply cease to exist after one year.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an answer along the same lines of your question. Anyone who thinks that something will happen that will destroy his investment will not go for that kind of thing. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. No further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Pusic's Defence doesn't have any questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Primorac. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am counsel for General Praljak here. I just have two small subjects to deal with. One question directly pertains to some of the things that you stated during the course of your testimony. Your Honours, I think that the first question would be belong to the category of pure cross-examination so I think that it should not be taken from my time afterwards. Mr. Primorac, you mentioned during your testimony this problem of workers' remittances or specifically pensions that many citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina received from foreign countries on the basis of their previous work abroad especially in Germany. In that context in order to enable the Trial Chamber to understand the gravity of the matter at that time in the former Yugoslavia and when Yugoslavia was breaking up in the first period of the war, workers' remittances was an expression that was bandied about. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber why this was an important category? What this was all about? Especially in terms of foreign currency? Also, could you tell us what it meant specifically for the economy of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from 1965, the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina could get passports more easily and go and work abroad. Most of them worked in Germany but there were others working in other countries, France, Switzerland, Austria, Sweden. Most of them went there to work for a temporary period of time in order to make more money to upgrade their family situation, increase their standard of living, et cetera. They stayed there and during the year they would come once or twice to visit their parents or their homeland. Throughout the year, they sent money to support their families so these were these remittances. These were very significant amounts from the point of view of the balance of payments of the country and also very significant amounts as a source of foreign currency for paying for the import of goods and all the other needs that existed in the state. The money that arrived in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, could be deposited in savings accounts or they were converted into dinars, financing the needs of the families of the persons who were employed abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just add one more thing in relation to that, perhaps. As a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina irrespective of all the high positions you held, you certainly knew because any average citizen would know, this same category of people, migrant workers as they were called, were they the people who helped their homeland, in this case, Bosnia and Herzegovina, through voluntary contributions, donations to their municipalities, to their own municipality in order to help secure weapons, humanitarian aid and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that such efforts were made by our people abroad and that resources were collected for defence purposes. I did not have experience with that kind of remittance so I am not in a position to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. And now, another group of questions that I will be using for a different purpose. And I believe that you will be able to answer these questions. Bearing in mind your CV or, rather, the line of work that you were involved in up until the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, my question would be as follows: Did you know Dr. Tanja Kesic?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know her and I still know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is it correct that Dr. Tanja Kesic was a professor at the University of Sarajevo, the school of economics?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that person is the sister of General Praljak who stands accused here?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Pero Kesic, her husband?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So he worked in Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he worked in Energoinvest and also at the school of machine engineering but also at the research and development institute of Energoinvest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Primorac. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Just two questions by way of a supplement, just for you to know exactly what the amounts of money were that were coming into Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the 1990s through these remittances and the amount in pensions which is another subgroup of the same thing and what that might today. These are the two questions that I would like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, are you competent in this field? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I'm qualified to ask this because I was a political enemy of the system that was in place at the time because they were hiding the amounts of money that were actually coming in and the extent to which the state subsisted based on those remittances coming in from abroad. I have been monitoring the situation for over two decades and I'm privy to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Based on your information, what were the amounts in terms of dollars of these remittances of migrant workers working abroad on average per year between 1965 and the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely can't answer that question because that information is not available to me; however, if you want that information, it should be available if you go to the original documents that were produced at the time and you can find it in documents published by The National Bank because they were in charge of foreign currency transactions. I certainly couldn't support your idea and your suggestion that this was being hidden because that was all open and all the transactions were recorded in the chequing account of the country itself and it should be easy enough to track this sort of information down, if you try hard enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I didn't say that this was being hidden systematically or that the national bank didn't exactly publish but it didn't publicise this. Nevertheless, according to your information from the 1980s, what were these workers' remittances that were being sent in to Bosnia and Herzegovina from somewhere abroad, what was the amount?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you expect me to extemporize. I simply don't have that information. I am a man who deals with stuff like that but whenever I encounter myself in a situation where I need specific information, I go back to the source, I study the source and I arrive at my information. Therefore my answer is the same as the previous one. You should go to the Bureau of the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It should be simple enough; maybe it's on the internet. It wasn't available then because there was no internet to speak of at the time but there are appropriate publications and I think this information is available in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that today's remittances of workers, migrant workers living abroad to Bosnia and Herzegovina are over 20 per cent of its budget?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slow down, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the remittances of migrant workers or people living abroad from the federation or part of Bosnia and Herzegovina today are over -- amount to over 20 per cent of the federation's overall budget?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm an economist. There is no room for improvisation in my profession. Firstly, this information can be obtained, what the remittances amount to in relation to the BH's overall budget. But I must remind you of one thing, these remittances don't go straight to the budget of Bosnia and Herzegovina; this is sent directly to families or rather the beneficiaries. The budget of Bosnia and Herzegovina is something that is accumulated or something that is replenished, if you like, from taxes, customs and other kinds of income. You have these two values and there may be a relation between them of some kind but there is no direct link.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Primorac, I said over 20 per cent of the budget, I didn't mean to imply that they were part of the budget or being sent into the budget but this is simply a cumulative amount of money and many people use this to get by. Thank you very much for your answers. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best to show exactly what these amounts were, remittances by workers from abroad for Yugoslavia, for Bosnia and Herzegovina, what the pensions were in such municipalities such as Livno and Orasje sometime in the late 1980s. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cross-examination is now over,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: for its own cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Dr. Primorac, good afternoon. I'm Pieter Kruger and as you gathered, I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. Sir, I see that from what you have just told General Praljak, you are an economist and as you said, there is no room for improvisation. I take it that you are not comfortable as a politician.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Economists deal in figures, no room for improvisation. Figures are always easy to prove. Politicians in that respect at least and that's the way I see it, have a situation that is somewhat easier because they deal in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the time that you were Minister of Finance, would that be fair to say that was virtually the only period that you had to function as a politician in some way?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, purely as a politician, although some of my previous positions, for example, the head of the chamber of commerce, although that was about economics, in essence, but in the former system, to some extent it had to do with politics as well. Therefore, throughout the previous period before I became minister, I did overlap with politics in one way or another from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you told the Court yesterday that you were never in the HDZ or were never a member of the HDZ; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you, however, in 1992, a member of the -- of another party, the SDP?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped being a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia after it was dissolved. If I may just remind you, the breakup of the party began in 1989 at what is known as the 14th Party Congress. All the republics, some at a faster pace, some at a lower one, disbanded their own party formations. Once I stopped being a member of the League of Communists I never joined another political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, how did it come that you were appointed Minister of Finance, to a political function?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with any debates at any of the Presidency meetings but I'll describe the process for you, how this worked. Jure Pelivan's government in April 1992 resigned. This was a period when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina commenced. There followed a period when there was no government at all. Formally they had resigned, the former Serb ministers left Sarajevo and there was a lot of speculation among the public as to who the new prime minister would be. It was always supposed to be a Croat though. Finally, I was called by the government, I had an interview and I suppose a decision that was eventually taken was for a number of people who had no political affiliations to become members of the government. People with no political links but people who enjoyed a high profile in Bosnia and Herzegovina from all three ethnic groups. That is how my late Serb friend Ugljesa Uzelac joined, he used to be the mayor of Sarajevo; writer Bruno Kolac; and then a Muslim also, Turajlic, who was not a member of any of the political parties, Asim Muratovic. As far as the Croats were concerned, I was there and Martin Raguz joined as well. As far as I know if you look at all the names that I've mentioned, as far as I know, Raguz was the only one who was a member of the liberal party. Aside from that, none of us others were members of any political parties or had any political affiliations at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I just check. Earlier you had said that you never, after the breakup of the League of Communists joined another political party; however, at page 87, line 16 and 17, you say that you were a member of the liberal party. Could you perhaps just explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which document you have in mind. I can't see that. Secondly, I was not a member of any party including the liberal party. I said that if you look at the names that I've mentioned, I assume that Raguz was the only one who was a member of the liberal party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I misread and I misheard. My apology. Was there any pressure or any attempts to get you to join the HDZ, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. What's more, I think the then leaders of the HDZ considered me to be somewhat of a leftist. I don't think they ever would have planned for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You are a Croat. Is there any reason or could you explain why you did not join the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a Croat, that's true. But there is no particular reason I never joined the HDZ. I never received an invitation. Even if I had, I wouldn't have done it all the same. Quite simply, I did not wish to have any form of political involvement. I explained that to Mr. Karnavas yesterday when he asked me why I had not been a member of the government and what my positions had been before the war. I preferred my own field of expertise. I preferred that over joining the HDZ or any other political party at the time, truth to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you say that the HDZ would have regarded you as somewhat of a leftist, does that imply that you did not necessarily agree with all the policies of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, anybody with my political beliefs at the time, the belief that it was no great fortune that we had national parties in power now, but it was a sign of the times. Those were the parties elected by the voters of Bosnia and Herzegovina and those parties were then given a mandate to put together a government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd very quickly like to just clear up one matter. If we can look at -- and this is in the binder that -- yes, thank you, the binder that you're just receiving. The document I wish to refer you to and so other people can also start looking for it is P 10504. Document P 10504. As you will see, this is a Reuters report by -- do you have it? By a Hugh Pain and it was an interview that was conducted with you around about 20 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, may I ask you by any chance do you have a Croatian copy of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies. If you turn two pages -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, we'll get back to the -- to this article in a bit more detail but the only thing I now wish to clear out with you is in the English version, if we turn to the second page, and on yours -- I'm just quickly checking in your version, you will see it's on page 3 of your version. There is a paragraph saying, "Emphasising" it reports what you said, "Primorac indicated that" and then it says, "Emphasising that the plan was his own" this is now for the reconstruction fund "and had not been adopted as official policy. Primorac, who retains his former post as vice-president, the Energoinvest industrial combine envisaged ..." and then it goes ahead. My question, sir, is at the time when this was -- when you gave this interview, you were already or you had just become the Minister of Finance of the BiH but is it correct, this, that you were also at that stage still vice-president of Energoinvest?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an operative sense, I wasn't, but if you want me to be as specific as I can as to my employment documents, my employment book, it stayed with the company with Energoinvest and it stayed that way all the way until March 1993 which is when my links with Energoinvest were eventually severed. So in a formal sense, yes, I was still their employee. But I was by this time already a full-time minister with the BH government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At this stage, were you still a professor or a lecturer at Sarajevo University or had you ended that part?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained a lecturer at the Sarajevo University until the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can move on to your career as Finance Minister, Minister of Finance. Yesterday, and for this, I don't know if it's necessary that you return to it but you were shown the decision that is in the Defence binder 1D 02645 and this was the decree by which you were appointed along with 16 other persons as Minister of Finance and 16 other people who were appointed as different ministers. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. But do I have it in the file in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's necessary that we look at it and what I would like to ask you: Apart from 16 persons being appointed as ministers, is it correct that 3 persons were appointed as vice prime ministers?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Mr. Turajlic, Simovic and Lagumdzija, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that the same document or by the same decision, Mr. Jure Pelivan was appointed as prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this group of people, would they have been known as the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To understand how this functioned, the executive would have been the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The Presidency, that was under the constitution. The Presidency, in a way, took over the function of the BH Assembly which was a legislative function because the assembly could not meet under those conditions. Nevertheless, the Presidency did have a number of executive powers, probably as concerned defence on behalf of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the executive body was the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and according to the same logic, the government in times of war as well. Apart from the fact that the constitution provides for certain functions, certain powers for the Presidency defence and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the cabinet was basically where the decisions were taken and from the cabinet, the decisions were implemented. What I'm referring to is basically the governance, the basic decisions for governing Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
