utterances.text: Let's try to see this matter through. The Assembly at the time could not pass any laws because it wasn't meeting, was it? One needed to inform -- to transform almost the entire legislative framework from a peacetime one to a wartime one. This is how the procedure worked. In order for the government to propose decree laws, and those proposed decree laws would then need to be ratified by the Presidency and as soon as the Presidency ratified them, the decree laws would take effect. So the government would propose laws and then after that during the implementation stage. So that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The cabinet, how regularly or did the cabinet meet, and I'm referring to it as cabinet for convenience. Did the cabinet meet in the initial phases when you were appointed, regularly, once a week, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the cabinet was meeting with far greater frequency but before I answer your question, please allow me another explanation. The government worked through its ministries, there were groups -- the three deputy prime ministers had the role of coordinating. Let me take the example of deputy minister Turajlic. He worked with ministries that had to do with the economy, the country's industry and so on and so forth. Coordination had nothing to do with the executive aspect of the government, the responsibility was ours, the ministers, but we had to coordinate among ourselves because sometimes there were conflicting interests and situations and then these proposals would be tabled to the government. That was the system according to which we worked at the time. There were other commissions and other bodies but that is not as important. How often were we meeting? Were we meeting? I think there were periods where we had daily meetings. This was a time of war and there were countless regulations that needed passing and needed processing at the time. All of that was difficult to get there at the time. My own office was at the national bank building, the distance from the government building being 300 metres. I'm not trying to get overemotional here but let me paint a picture for you. There were certain situations where it was simply impossible for me to cross the 300 metres simply because we were being showered by bullets at all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I can imagine that it was difficult to get all those ministers together. I understand the situation. Sir, under those circumstances when there were, for instance, daily meetings, how would it be notified that there was a meeting? Would it be a preset time and place or would ministers be given an agenda and summoned to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, materials would be prepared, a whole pile of those in fact. Depending on their nature, they had to go through this coordination procedure that I told you about and then that would go to the government. More often than not, the next meeting would be scheduled at each of the meetings. If all of the materials had not been sorted yet, they would be delivered by one of the drivers in due course and they would be waiting for us at our tables as soon as we came to a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The prime minister, did he normally chair these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a rule whenever he was in Sarajevo. The period that I'm talking about when I was physically there, I think he was twice away from Sarajevo which is where the appropriate deputy would stand in for him. More often than not, this was Mr. Turajlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, how did it function when -- or what was the procedure when somebody was away from Sarajevo on official business or unable to attend, would that person, a minister or a deputy, would that person designate somebody else to attend the meetings in his or her stead?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever a minister was away for whatever reason, it was customary for his or her deputy to appear at the government meeting. This was very much the established practice. However, if even the deputy was unable to attend, then the third in command, so to speak, would need authorisation to attend a government meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what about the minister who is at the top of that ministry's pyramid who was away? Would he at least coordinate with his deputy or then the third person who was going to attend to give some feedback on his or her own activities away from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this worked in the other ministries, but I can tell you about mine. I had very close cooperation with my own deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of your deputy?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muhamed Logo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what was he, was he a deputy minister or ...

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you appoint him yourself or was he also appointed by decision?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the power to appoint him. He was appointed -- well, I can't be certain but I think both the ministers and the deputies were appointed by the Presidency. If not, it was a government decision. It certainly wasn't within my power to make that sort of appointment. There is something else you need to bear in mind though. At the time, one thing that was always taken into account was the ethnic breakdown if you looked at the top-ranking positions in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We tried to achieve some sort of a balance. If the minister was a Croat such as I was, his deputy would be a Muslim, or the other way around. We tried to achieve this sort of balance. This was very much the established practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in the few minutes remaining, just for a further basis for understanding your position, I'd like to ask you a little bit about how your -- what the structure of your department was or your ministry. You were the minister, you had a deputy minister. What was beneath you? You referred to the Ministry of Finance being in the banka building or the bank building. Could you just describe the structure briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, small correction, the ministry was not in the bank building, my office was. The ministry was in the same building but opposite the entrance and my office was in the central wing of the building. Apart from the deputy, there was several assistants there as well. I don't know how many. Probably a total of four or five. They were in charge of certain sectors. For example, there was an assistant for budgetary issues. There was a customs assistant, a banking assistant. That sort of thing. There were several assistants who covered various fields of the ministry's activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And perhaps just a final question for today, I think, or final topic. So these assistants, they were basically the managers but if you went down from them, you would probably go into the various offices of the Department of Finance throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZARKO PRIMORAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once you went below that level, there were department heads or sector heads, if you like. Most of the activity took place in Sarajevo; however, there was services and sub-ministries of the finance ministry and there were certain outposts, so to speak. I would need to think back and think hard to remember exactly how this worked and explain that to you, but there were certain sections of the ministry, the customs section, for example, and those had to be outposts, they had to be elsewhere and not in Sarajevo by virtue of their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to stop now, Mr. Kruger. There is another hearing after us and I'm involved myself in another trial. It's almost quarter to 2.00. Witness, we shall meet again tomorrow morning. I trust that you will be able to leave afterwards and that you will not have to wait until next week. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 9.00. ---Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m. to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of June, 2008 at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
